title: Grounding and citation
story:
Grounding is the requirement that an answer be derivable from text you supplied, rather than from whatever the model absorbed in training. Citation is the requirement that each claim point at the passage it came from. They are different requirements, and a system can satisfy the second while failing the first, which is the whole problem.

Think about where a citation comes from. The model produces it the same way it produces everything else: by continuing plausibly. Asked for a reference, it will emit something reference-shaped, because reference-shaped text is what follows a claim in the material it learned from. The shape of a citation carries no information about whether the passage supports the claim, or whether the passage was read, or in the worst case whether it exists.

So the rule is short. An unverified citation is decoration, and decoration that buys trust is worse than nothing.

That last clause is the part to take seriously, because it inverts the usual instinct. Citations change how people read. A cited answer is checked less carefully than an uncited one — the reader takes the reference as evidence that someone did the work. Adding unverified citations to a system therefore increases the harm it can do, because it has bought credibility it did not earn. If you cannot verify them, you are better off without them.

Verification is mechanical, which is the good news. Have the model quote a span from the passage it is citing, and then check that the span appears in that passage, character for character. If it does not appear, you have caught it before the reader did, and you can drop the claim, drop the citation, or fail the whole answer, depending on what the system is for. This is cheap, it runs in code rather than in a prompt, and it converts an assurance into a check.

Keep one distinction clear while you build it. Retrieved is not used. A system that attaches every passage it retrieved is telling you what it read, not what the answer rests on, and a reader who follows those references finds a pile of related material with no way to know which line mattered. A citation is a claim about provenance for one statement, so tie it to a statement, not to the response.

On the cost, be honest with yourself about what you are trading. Requiring verbatim quotes constrains the writing and makes answers longer and blockier. Checking strictly will reject legitimate paraphrase, and a good answer will sometimes be thrown away because it restated the source in better words than the source used. You are choosing which error you prefer, and for almost anything consequential the choice is easy: a clunky answer that is checkable beats a smooth answer that might be invented.

There is one more thing worth building in, because it is the case people forget. The honest answer is sometimes that the supplied passages do not contain what was asked for. A grounded system must be able to say so, and it will not do that by itself — the pattern of a question followed by an answer is overwhelming, and the model will assemble something from whatever is nearest. Make the absence of support an allowed output, test for it with questions whose answers you have deliberately left out of the corpus, and you will learn quickly whether your grounding is real or whether it has been paraphrasing the nearest paragraph all along.

problem.name: Provenance for a generated claim
problem.shape: An answer has to be traceable to supplied evidence, and the thing producing the answer also produces the references.
tell: the references are generated in the same pass as the prose and never checked
every retrieved passage is attached to the response rather than to a statement

problem.move: Require a verbatim span with each claim, check the span against the cited passage in code, and tie each citation to a statement rather than to the whole response. Make the absence of support a first-class output and test for it deliberately.
problem.invariant: A citation is only evidence if something other than the generator confirmed the cited passage contains the quoted span.
problem.breaks: Unverified citations raise trust without raising accuracy, so adding them makes the system more dangerous than it was — and strict verification rejects legitimate paraphrase, which is the error you are choosing to accept.

cost.time: an extra check per claim, in code rather than in the model, which is cheap and adds a step to every answer
cost.space: verbatim quotes lengthen the output and constrain the writing, making answers blockier than they would otherwise be
cost.beats: asking the model to be honest in the prompt, which is a request rather than a mechanism, and attaching everything retrieved, which reports reading rather than use

worked.problem: Why is an unverified citation worse than no citation at all?

problem.practice: Take your system's last ten cited answers and check every quoted span against its source by hand. Count how many do not appear. Whatever that number is, it is the number your readers have been trusting, and it is the strongest argument you will ever have for putting the check in code.

beats.broke: The thing generating the answer also generates the references, and a reference produced by continuing plausibly carries no evidence that the passage supports the claim or even exists.
beats.fix: Require a verbatim span per claim and check it against the cited passage in code, tying each citation to a statement rather than to the response.
beats.cost: Quoting constrains the writing and strict checking rejects good paraphrase, which is the error you accept in exchange for answers that can be checked at all.

interview.q: Why is an unverified citation worse than no citation at all?
interview.trap: Thinking of citations as a transparency feature. They are a trust multiplier, so attaching unverified ones raises credibility without raising accuracy, and that gap is where the harm is.
interview.answer:
Because it buys trust it has not earned. The model produces a citation the same way it produces prose — by continuing plausibly — so asked for a reference it emits something reference-shaped, and the shape says nothing about whether the passage supports the claim, whether it was read, or whether it exists.

Meanwhile citations change how people read: a cited answer gets checked less carefully, because the reference looks like evidence that someone did the work. So unverified references raise credibility without raising accuracy, and the system becomes more dangerous than it was. Without verification I would rather ship no citations.

Verification is mechanical, which is why there is no excuse for skipping it: have the model quote a span from the passage it cites, then check in code that the span appears there character for character, and drop the claim or fail the answer when it does not.

I would also keep retrieved separate from used — attaching everything retrieved reports what was read, not what the answer rests on, and leaves the reader unable to tell which line mattered. Provenance belongs on the statement.

The cost I accept knowingly: verbatim quoting makes answers longer and blockier, and strict checking sometimes rejects a good paraphrase. For anything consequential, a clunky checkable answer beats a smooth one that might be invented.

And I would build in the case people forget — that the passages sometimes do not contain the answer. That has to be an allowed output, and the way to find out whether it works is to ask questions whose answers were deliberately left out of the corpus.

GROUNDING vs CITATION

  grounding: the answer is DERIVABLE FROM SUPPLIED TEXT
  citation:  each claim POINTS AT ITS PASSAGE
  a system can DO THE SECOND AND FAIL THE FIRST

WHERE A CITATION COMES FROM

  the same place as the prose: PLAUSIBLE CONTINUATION
  reference-shaped text IS NOT EVIDENCE

THE INVERSION WORTH HOLDING

  citations make readers CHECK LESS.
  unverified ones RAISE TRUST WITHOUT RAISING ACCURACY.
  -> they make the system MORE DANGEROUS, not less.

THE CHECK

  QUOTE A SPAN -> CONFIRM IT APPEARS, CHARACTER FOR
  CHARACTER
  in CODE, not in A PROMPT
  fails -> drop the claim, or fail the answer

  RETRIEVED IS NOT USED. cite THE STATEMENT, not THE
  RESPONSE.

THE TRADE

  quoting is CLUNKIER | strict checking REJECTS GOOD
  PARAPHRASE
  choose the error: CHECKABLE AND CLUNKY beats SMOOTH
  AND MAYBE INVENTED

THE FORGOTTEN CASE

  the passages MAY NOT CONTAIN THE ANSWER.
  make that AN ALLOWED OUTPUT and TEST IT ON PURPOSE.
takeaway: A model produces citations the same way it produces prose, so an unverified citation is decoration that makes readers check less — quote a span, confirm it appears in the cited passage in code, attach provenance to statements rather than responses, and make no-support an allowed answer you test for.
